entries.clue: Sticky quality that’s characteristic of seafood? (10)

blocks.note: the damp, tacky feel of cold sweaty skin
the question mark invites a made-up noun: the quality of being like a particular shellfish

annotation.surface: Someone describing the texture of a plate of shellfish.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the invented sense: 'clamminess' reread as the quality a clam has.
annotation.definitionFit: Clamminess is an unpleasant damp stickiness, as of skin.

entries.clue: At first, celebration agreeable – before Everyman showed up (4)

indicatorNotes.At first: take the opening letter of each following word
indicatorNotes.before: the first letters come ahead of the next piece

blocks.note: first letters of celebration and agreeable
the setter refers to himself as ME

annotation.surface: A party was pleasant until the crossword setter turned up.
annotation.walkthrough: A setter naming himself in a clue usually means ME or I; here Everyman is ME.
annotation.definitionFit: To come is to show up, so 'came' is 'showed up'.

entries.clue: Primarily, architectural polygonal / semicircular exhedra? (4)

indicatorNotes.Primarily: take the first letter of each following word

blocks.note: first letters of the four words

annotation.surface: An architecture glossary entry for a curved recess.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue does both jobs: the first letters spell the answer, and the words describe it.
annotation.definitionFit: An apse is a semicircular or polygonal recess, typically at the east end of a church; an exedra is a similar recess.

entries.clue: Ones on the wing in derisory prison (11)

annotation.definitionNote: the plural 'Ones' stands for the singular answer, read as the species

blocks.note: derisory = mocking
bird is British slang for a prison sentence, as in 'doing bird'

annotation.surface: Prisoners in one wing of a jail being jeered at.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wing' looks like a prison block, which is exactly where the surface wants you; it is the bird's wing.
annotation.definitionFit: Mockingbirds are birds, creatures on the wing.

entries.clue: Wrote symbols, number 500, describing gallery (7)

indicatorNotes.describing: to describe is to draw around, so NO…D goes around the gallery

blocks.note: abbreviation of number
D is the Roman numeral for 500
the Tate, the London art gallery

annotation.surface: Someone numbering the exhibits while writing about a gallery.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Describing' is used in its geometric sense of drawing a line around something.
annotation.definitionFit: To notate is to write something down in symbols, as in music.

entries.clue: Star with radiant smile that’s matey (7)

annotation.definitionNote: 'matey' is the noun, a friendly form of address, as 'sunbeam' is

blocks.note: the sun is a star
a beam is a broad smile

annotation.surface: A celebrity with a winning grin who is also friendly.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain 'sunbeam' is a jokey, familiar way to address someone, like 'matey' or 'mate'. 'Star' looks like a celebrity but is the astronomical kind.
annotation.definitionFit: Both 'sunbeam' and 'matey' are cheery British terms of address to a man.

entries.clue: Pointedly cut back? That’s crazy (4)

indicatorNotes.back: to go back is to return the way you came, so the letters are read from the end to the start

blocks.note: to stab is to cut with a point

annotation.surface: Someone scoffing at the idea of pruning something to a point.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cut back' reads as one phrase meaning prune, but 'back' is the reversal instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Bats, as in 'bats in the belfry', is informal for mad.

entries.clue: In stoic fashion, lab cats try to run free (10)

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

annotation.surface: Laboratory cats calmly attempting an escape.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: doing something abstractly, detached from the moment, is close to doing it stoically.
annotation.definitionFit: Abstractly means in a detached, removed way, as a stoic keeps feeling at a distance.

entries.clue: Wears checks where drinks are sold (6,4)

blocks.note: to sport a tie is to wear it
to bar is to check or block

annotation.surface: A dress code note: tartan is worn in the pub.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Checks' looks like the pattern that goes with 'wears'; it is the verb meaning stops.
annotation.definitionFit: Sports bars are pubs with games on screens, places where drinks are sold.

entries.clue: It may take notes for one on the fiddle (5,5)

annotation.definition: It may take notes for one on the fiddle

blocks.note: the surface suggests jotting things down; the setter means holding sheet music
the surface suggests a swindler; the setter means a violinist

annotation.surface: A fraudster's accomplice keeping written records of a scam.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On the fiddle' suggests fraud, and 'take notes' suggests writing things down; really it holds sheet music for a violinist.
annotation.definitionFit: A music stand holds the sheet music a violinist reads.

entries.clue: ‘European capital?’ ‘Cairo, Slovenia.’ ‘… not entirely’ (4)

indicatorNotes.not entirely: the answer is only part of the words given

blocks.note: cairO SLOvenia

annotation.surface: A quiz exchange in which the contestant gives two wrong capitals.
annotation.walkthrough: Cairo is not in Europe and Slovenia is a country, so the reply is 'not entirely' right, which is also the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Oslo, Norway's capital, is one European capital, and the question mark admits there are others.

entries.clue: Tired? I’ll trot out something to read (6,6)

indicatorNotes.out: the letters are put out of order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters

annotation.surface: Someone offering a weary friend a book to pick up.
annotation.walkthrough: Little Dorrit is a Dickens novel.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: any book will do, and this one is a Charles Dickens novel of 1857.

entries.clue: Men with pointers meddled – everywhere you look! (11)

indicatorNotes.meddled: the letters are interfered with and mixed

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters; 'with' joins the two words

annotation.surface: A complaint that interfering men with pointing sticks are everywhere.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is a phrase meaning the same as the adjective: something omnipresent is everywhere you look.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain paraphrase: the Latin 'omni' means all, so the word describes something found in every place at once.

entries.clue: Isolates unhealthy Easter eggs … (10)

indicatorNotes.unhealthy: the letters are in a bad state, so rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

annotation.surface: A health-conscious parent setting chocolate eggs apart.
annotation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links the surface to 14 down; it has no job in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: To segregate is to set apart, to isolate.

entries.clue: … so quietly, went on to say … ‘chubby’ (4-6)

blocks.note: 'so' and 'well' both open a remark
p = piano, quietly in music
to add is to go on to say

annotation.surface: Continuing 13 down: someone murmurs that eating all those eggs leaves you chubby.
annotation.walkthrough: The ellipses carry on the story from 13 down; each clue is solved on its own.
annotation.definitionFit: Well-padded is a jokey way of saying plump.

entries.clue: European, and united, it’s become apparent (7)

blocks.note: E = European
merged = joined together

annotation.surface: News that Europe has come together.
annotation.walkthrough: 'It's become apparent' is 'it's emerged', so the past participle matches.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the reporting sense: news that comes to light, as in 'it later came out', surfaces into view.

entries.clue: Section of symposium in ICA building that may transport you (7)

annotation.definitionNote: a relative clause standing for the noun: a thing that may transport you

indicatorNotes.Section of: the answer is a section of the words that follow

blocks.note: symposiuM IN ICA Building

annotation.surface: Part of a conference at the ICA, a London arts centre, proves moving.
annotation.walkthrough: The ICA is the Institute of Contemporary Arts in London. 'Transport' looks like being moved emotionally; a minicab is a British private hire taxi.
annotation.definitionFit: A minicab is a hired car that carries passengers.

entries.clue: Perks up demonstrations (7)

blocks.note: a verb: recovers strength or spirits, as a sick patient does
a plural noun: mass public meetings or protest marches

annotation.surface: Protest marches lift the spirits.
annotation.walkthrough: The two definitions use different parts of speech: 'Perks up' is a verb and 'demonstrations' a plural noun, and one word covers both.
annotation.definitionFit: To rally is to recover strength; a rally is a mass meeting or protest.

entries.clue: River around north’s quiet presently (7)

indicatorNotes.around: one thing placed around another encloses it, so the word for presently wraps the letter for north

blocks.note: sh! = be quiet
anon = soon, presently
N = north, placed inside ANON

annotation.surface: A river bend where the north side will soon go quiet.
annotation.walkthrough: The Shannon is the longest river in Ireland. 'Presently' is the old sense 'soon', not 'now'.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Shannon, flowing through the middle of Ireland to the Atlantic, is one river among many.

entries.clue: Hot and bothered, with fourth and fifth characters quitting playgroup (7)

indicatorNotes.bothered: the letters are agitated and rearranged
indicatorNotes.quitting: the named letters leave the word

blocks.clueFragment: with fourth and fifth characters quitting playgroup
blocks.note: PLAYGROUP loses its fourth and fifth letters, Y and G

annotation.surface: A flustered child leaves playgroup.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hot and bothered' reads as one flustered phrase, but it splits: 'Hot' is the definition and 'bothered' stirs the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal sense: a 'hot' ticket or band is one everyone wants, much in demand and widely liked.

entries.clue: Feel uncomfortable following roast: dash! (7)

indicatorNotes.following: what follows something comes after it, so the word for feeling uncomfortable goes after the word for roast

blocks.note: to roast a play is to pan it, criticise it harshly
to ache is to hurt

annotation.surface: Someone who has overeaten at a roast dinner needs to rush off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Roast' looks like the Sunday meal; it is the verb meaning criticise.
annotation.definitionFit: Dash and panache both mean stylish flair.

entries.clue: Terrific Hitchcock thriller with a drop of red sauce (5,7)

indicatorNotes.a drop of: just one letter, the first, of red

blocks.note: grand = splendid
Marnie, the 1964 Hitchcock film
first letter of red

annotation.surface: A great Hitchcock film with a splash of red, fake blood, in it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sauce' looks like something for food, but it is slang for alcohol; Grand Marnier is an orange liqueur.
annotation.definitionFit: The sauce is slang for alcoholic drink, and Grand Marnier is a liqueur.

entries.clue: Double the size of your dating pool in inhospitable location? (4)

annotation.definition2: Double the size of your dating pool

blocks.clueFragment: Double the size of your dating pool
blocks.note: a two-word instruction: start dating both men and women
a vast, cold desert in Mongolia and northern China

annotation.surface: Dating advice for someone stuck somewhere remote.
annotation.walkthrough: The first half is a whimsical phrase, GO BI, meaning become bisexual, which doubles the people you might date.
annotation.definitionFit: The Gobi is a desert in Mongolia and China, about as inhospitable as places get.

entries.clue: Does a mafioso’s job on old fellow, vacantly fearless (4)

indicatorNotes.vacantly: with the inside emptied out, leaving only the outer letters

blocks.note: O = old
F = fellow
outer letters of fearless

annotation.surface: A gangster fearlessly carrying out a hit on an elderly man.
annotation.walkthrough: To off someone is slang for killing them, the gangster's job.
annotation.definitionFit: Offs is slang for kills, the task of a mafia hitman.

entries.clue: In retirement, make some changes? It’s regularly seen, in the main (4)

annotation.definition: It’s regularly seen, in the main

indicatorNotes.In retirement: to retire is to draw back, so the word goes backwards

blocks.note: to edit is to make changes

annotation.surface: A retired person tinkering with things, and something seen regularly at sea.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The main' is an old word for the open sea, and the tide comes in regularly there. 'Regularly' tempts you to take alternate letters, but none spell TIDE.
annotation.definitionFit: The tide rises and falls at regular intervals in the sea.

entries.clue: Finished, being hot (7,3)

blocks.note: to knock off is to stop work for the day
slang for stolen, as hot goods are

annotation.surface: Someone done in by the heat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hot' is slang for stolen, and 'knocked off' is British slang for stolen too.
annotation.definitionFit: You knock off when finished work, and stolen goods are knocked off.

entries.clue: Expressed weariness, heard in TV station (4)

indicatorNotes.heard: the word is as it sounds, not as it is written

blocks.note: a past-tense verb for letting out a tired breath, said aloud

annotation.surface: A tired sound picked up in a television studio.
annotation.walkthrough: In British slang a TV channel is a 'side', as in 'what's on the other side?'.
annotation.definitionFit: Side is dated British slang for a TV channel.

entries.clue: Harbours’ charms (10)

blocks.note: to entertain an idea is to harbour it
to entertain is to amuse, to charm

annotation.surface: The attractions of seaside ports.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe makes both words look like nouns; ignore it and read both as verbs.
annotation.definitionFit: Harbours and charms both mean entertains: holds in mind, and delights.
